The importance of such objects in circulating the visual ideas and styles of artists and the changing status of printmakers as makers will serve as guiding themes.

subject: ARTH
title: Art and Image in the Age of Pharaohs
description: Explores four thousand years of Egyptian art form the building of the Great Pyramids and the splendor of the New Kingdom to the achievements of its Hellenistic successors and beyond. Focuses on royal monuments, images of life, death, and afterlife along the Nile, mummies and funerary art, religion and temples, sculpture, luxury arts as well as objects of everyday life.

subject: ARTH
title: Art of South and Southeast Asia
description: Survey of the art and architecture of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. The major achievements of each period are examined in relation to their religious, political, and social contexts.

subject: ARTH
title: Art of China: Neolithic Period Through the Song Dynasty
description: Survey of the art and architecture of China up through the 13th century including early bronze-casting, funerary arts, Buddhist arts, painting, and ceramics. Selected major monuments are examined in relation to their religious, political, and social contexts.

subject: ARTH
title: Art of China: Yuan through Qing Dynasties
description: Survey of the art and architecture of China from the fourteenth through the nineteenth centuries including painting, religious and secular architecture, woodblock prints, and ceramics. subject: ARTH
title: Chinese Art of the 20th and 21st Centuries
description: Survey of Chinese art from the late 19th century through the present. Hong Kong, Taiwanese, and expatriate artists are also considered.

subject: ARTH

description: Survey of the art and architecture of Japan from the Neolithic period to the 19th century. The major achievements of each period are examined in relation to their religious, political, and social contexts.

subject: ARTH

subject: ENGL
title: Introduction to Middle English
description: A survey of the language and literature of England from the 12th through the 15th centuries. Reading of prose works and shorter poetry will be done in Middle English with special attention paid to grammar, style, dialect, and language change. The class will explore the culture of medieval England through critical essays, histories, and supplementary texts in translation. (RE) Prerequisite(s): ENGL

subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL
title: Shakespeare II: Later Plays

(RE) Prerequisite(s): ENGL 102* , ENGL 112* , ENGL 132* , or ENGL 298*

subject: ENGL
title: Shakespeare’s Contemporaries: Renaissance Drama

subject: ENGL
title: Late Eighteenth-Century British Literature

subject: ENGL
title: The 19th-Century British Novel

subject: ENGL
title: Modern British Novel

subject: ENGL
title: Jane Austen

subject: ENGL
title: American Realism and Naturalism

subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL

subject: ENGL

(RE) Corequisite(s): FINC 475 Registration Restriction(s): Majors in the Haslam College of Business

subject: FINC

description: Decision-making topics in financial management, including valuation, capital budgeting under uncertainty, cost of capital, capital structure theory, and dividend policy. Major writing requirement. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 420 or FINC 428 with grades of C or better. (RE) Corequisite(s): FINC 425 or FINC 427 . Registration Restriction(s): Majors in the Haslam College of Business.

subject: FINC
title: Honors: Financial Management, Theory and Practice
description: Decision-making topics in financial management, including valuation, capital budgeting under uncertainty, cost of capital, capital structure theory, and dividend policy. Major writing requirement. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306 or FINC 308 and FINC 420 or FINC 428 with a grade of B or better. (RE) Corequisite(s): FINC 425 or FINC 427 .

subject: FINC

description: Introduces students to the world of FinTech (Financial Technology). The course spends significant time on one of the most disruptive innovations in FinTech – blockchain technology. subject: FINC

description: Spotlights the financial analysis of various products and services historically found in traditional banking. Registration Restriction(s): Majors in the Haslam College of Business.

subject: FINC
title: Insurance and Financial Planning Management
description: Course will cover the basic principles of risk management; insurance; and financial, estate and retirement planning. For students interested, an optional component of the class may include material for property and casualty pre-licensing education. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306, FINC 308, or FINC 351 with grade of C or better. Registration Restriction(s): Majors in the Haslam College of Business.

subject: FINC
title: Real Estate Finance and Investment Analysis
description: Explores the major concepts, principles, analytical methods, and tools used to evaluate the financing of and investment in real property. Emphasis is also placed on understanding the factors influencing the dynamics of commercial real estate markets. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306 or FINC 308 and FINC 381 with grades of C or better.

subject: FINC
title: Real Estate Cases
description: Builds upon knowledge and skills from other real estate coursework in applied analysis of “real world” assets and case studies. Includes in-depth market analysis, financial analysis, and presentation of results. Students will be introduced to data sources and widely used software, interact with speakers from industry, and submit work to regional, national, or international case competitions. (RE)

subject: FINC
title: Securities Industry Essentials Prep
description: Self-paced preparatory course for the Securities Industry Essentials Exam. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306 with grade of C or better. Registration Restriction(s): Majors in the Haslam College of Business

subject: FINC
title: Finance Help Desk
description: Hold “Help Desk” hours and assist students currently enrolled in Finance courses. Repeatability: Repeatable up to 3 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 301 , FINC 306 , or FINC 308 .

subject: FINC
title: Off-Campus Study
description: Professional internship with practicing professionals under the direction of a faculty member. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306 or FINC 308 with grade of C or better. Comment(s): Finance majors only. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: FINC
title: Independent Study
description: Grading Restriction: Letter grade only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 hours. Comment(s): Finance majors only. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: FINC
title: Bloomberg Basics
description: This proprietary training course teaches students how to navigate the Bloomberg terminal, download data in Excel, and analyze data in four market sectors: Equities, Fixed Income, Forex, and Commodities. These skills are applicable in future coursework and/or on the job site. (RE) Corequisite(s): FINC 301 or FINC 306 .

subject: FINC
title: Investment Fund Management
description: Students manage a portfolio(s) of real dollars and have fiduciary responsibility regarding same. Emphasis is on decisions that must be made by and/or for the ultimate investor using analytical tools and empirical evidence. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 4 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FINC 306 or FINC 308 with a grade of B+ or better; FINC 420 or FINC 428 with a grade of B+ or better. (RE)

subject: FINC
title: Bloomberg Applications
description: This is a proprietary training program designed for students to gather, describe, and analyze data on a Bloomberg terminal, with a focus on experiential learning. Bloomberg terminals and Excel API will be utilized to illustrate how data analytics can improve financial decision-making. subject: FORS
title: Forests and Forestry in American Society
description: Introductory course examining the role of forests in shaping American culture and society and exploring the evolution of the forestry profession in North America.

subject: FORS
title: The Science of Tree Climbing
description: This course will provide an in-depth exploration of arboriculture, the science and practice of how to manage, and care for trees, shrubs, and other perennial woody plants. Students will examine the biological principles underlying tree growth and health. Through a combination of theoretical study and practical application, the course covers key aspects of arboriculture, including pruning, fertiliz

subject: FORS
title: Tree Biology
description: An introduction to the anatomy and development of woody plants, their reproduction, growth requirements, and functioning. (RE) Prerequisite(s): BIOL 101* , BIOL 113* , or BIOL 150* .

subject: FORS
title: Forest Ecology
description: Ecological interactions among tree species, other plant and animal species, and their environment. Forest ecosystem classification; energy, nutrient, and hydrologic cycles; and site quality. Perturbations and growth, survival and forest composition; forest succession; and fire ecology. Regeneration ecology through establishment and stand dynamics. Physiological ecology, ecological strategies, and

subject: FORS
title: Honors: Tree Biology
description: Students will attend FORS 214 classes with supplementary assignments. (RE) Prerequisite(s): BIOL 101* , BIOL 113* , or BIOL 150* .

subject: FORS
title: Prescribed Fire Management
description: Prescribed fire ecology, use, and management in forest stands. Grading Restriction: Letter grade only. (RE) Prerequisite(s): SNR 312 .

subject: FORS
title: Economics of Forest and Wildland Resources
description: Basic principles of forest resource economics, finance, and valuation. Microeconomic applications for forestry and natural resources. Financial analysis of private and public natural resource management decisions. (DE) Prerequisite(s): AREC 201* or ECON 201* , ECON 211* , or ECON 213* .

subject: FORS
title: Honors: Economics of Forest and Wildland Resources
description: Students will attend FORS 314 classes with supplementary assignments. (DE) Prerequisite(s): ECON 201*

subject: FORS
title: Wildland Recreation
description: Introduction to Wildland Recreation: Historical and philosophical foundations of recreation, wildland recreation behavior, resources, policy, planning and management, and natural history interpretation.

subject: FORS
title: Silvicultural Practices
description: Application of silvicultural techniques and tree improvement. Use of herbicides and fire management.

subject: FORS
title: People and Forest Practices
description: Examination of how people, institutions, and society at large affect and are affected by forest management practices. Case studies and field applications will concentrate on the wide variety of linkages that exist in society among people and forests. Application of basic skills of collaborative problem solving will be emphasized. Overnight field trips are required. Grading Restriction: Letter grad

subject: FORS
title: Honors: Wildland Recreation
description: Students will attend FORS 321* classes with supplementary assignments.

subject: FORS
title: Forest Resource Inventory
description: Tree, log, and lumber scaling and grading. Land inventory and stand mapping. Volume estimation. (RE) Prerequisite(s): SNR 313 . (RE) Corequisite(s): FORS 323 .

subject: FORS
title: Wood Science
description: A survey of the anatomy, properties, applications, and impacts of wood materials. Includes training in wood identification. Recommended for foresters, engineers, architects, materials scientists, and anyone with an interest in this important natural resource.

subject: FORS
title: Forest Products Industry
description: An overview of the many steps in wood products manufacturing, from forest harvest to finished products. Includes visits to industrial facilities. (RE) Corequisite(s): FORS 322* and FORS 323 .

subject: FORS
title: Principles of Urban Forestry
description: Introductory course covers the history of the urban forest, benefits and costs of urban forests, tree biology, urban soil, urban forestry planning and management, urban forestry and public policy, and public works.

subject: FORS
title: Honors: Wood Properties and Uses
description: Students will attend FORS 331 classes with supplementary assignments.

subject: FORS
title: Practical Arboriculture
description: Students will be exposed to modern hands-on techniques in arboriculture that will demonstrate real-world situations and teach students to respond appropriately. Techniques covered will include climbing, cabling, bracing, and pruning.

subject: FORS
title: Principles of Wood Procurement and Forest Operations
description: An introduction to wood procurement, forest road building, and harvest planning. Topics will include different procurement methods, financial and resource assessment, negotiation skills, and legal requirements of wood procurement; basic forest hydrology and road construction concepts; and harvest technology and planning.

subject: FORS
title: Forest Harvesting
description: Introduction to forest harvesting techniques, best management practices, and environmental and social considerations regarding forest harvesting. (RE) Prerequisite(s): SNR 312

subject: FORS
title: Tree Physiology
description: Tree structure, growth, development, function, and how these are related to the environment and to cultural practices. Influence of environmental variables on plant growth and distribution. Effects of forest management practices on growth and function. Credit Restriction: Students may not receive credit for both FORS 414 and FORS 514. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FORS 214 or BIOL 114* .

subject: FORS
title: Forest Resource Management
description: Introduction to forest-level management concepts from an economic perspective. Harvest determination; goal setting under multiple-use concepts; taxes; classical approaches to regulation, linear programming and harvest scheduling; and goal programming. (DE) Prerequisite(s): FORS 100 or WFS 100 .

subject: FORS
title: Forest and Wildland Resource Policy
description: Policy formulation and criteria for policy determination. Forest and wildland law and regulation. Theory of conflict resolution. Formal and informal resolution. (DE) Prerequisite(s): FORS 100 or WFS 100 . Registration Restriction(s): Minimum student level – senior.

subject: FORS
title: Wildland Recreation Planning and Management
description: Planning processes, master and site planning, and site design projects. Management strategies and methods of visitor and recreation site management. Case studies. Weekend field trips may be required. Contact Hour Distribution: 2 hours and 1 lab.

subject: FORS
title: Honors: Forest Resource Management
description: Students will attend FORS 420 classes with supplementary assignments.

subject: FORS
title: Urbanization and Urban Soils
description: Course will cover the below-ground factors that affect tree establishment and survival in urban areas, specifically addressing the importance of soil structure, density, pH, water availability, and chemical properties (i.e. minerals, CEC).

subject: FORS
title: Trees and the Law
description: Course will evaluate tree law cases in the United States, focusing primarily on tree problems between private neighbors, government, and public utilities. (DE) Prerequisite(s): FORS 100 or WFS 100 .

subject: FORS
title: Practicum in Forestry
description: Supervised experience at departmental-approved employment location. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. Registration Restriction(s): Minimum student level – junior.

subject: FORS
title: Independent Study in Forestry
description: Special research or individual problem in forestry. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 15 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: FORS
title: Internship in Wildland Recreation
description: A highly-structured field experience guided by specific learning objectives. Students earn one credit per two weeks of full-time field experience. The student is responsible for field placement. Must be pre-approved by the instructor and the field supervisor. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. Registration Restriction(s): Minimum student level – junior.

subject: FORS
title: Internship in Forestry
description: Supervised experience at departmental-approved employment location arranged by the student. Students earn one credit per two weeks of full-time field experience. Internship learning objectives must be pre-approved by the advisor/instructor and the field supervisor. Daily log, supervisor evaluations, and final report required.

subject: FREN
title: Elementary French I
description: Introduction to French. Grading Restriction: ABC/N grading only. Credit Restriction: Not available to students eligible for FREN 150 or higher.

subject: FREN
title: Elementary French II
description: Introduction to French. Grading Restriction: ABC/N grading only. Credit Restriction: Not available to students eligible for FREN 150. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FREN 111 with grade of C or better or departmental placement exam.

subject: FREN

subject: FREN

description: This course offers an introduction to the history, geography, politics, and society of the Francophone world. subject: FREN

subject: FREN

subject: FREN

subject: FREN
title: Honors: Intermediate French II
description: For students of superior ability in French. Students follow enriched program with emphasis on speaking ability and reading, including literary selections.

subject: FREN
title: Elements of French for Upper-Division and Graduate Students
description: Elements of language, elementary and advanced readings. Grading Restriction: No auditors. Credit Restriction: No credit for students who have completed FREN 111 - FREN 112 or equivalent. Comment(s): Open to graduate students (for undergraduate credit) preparing for language examinations and upper-division students desiring reading knowledge of the language.

subject: FREN
title: Intermediate Composition and Grammar
description: Emphasizes writing skills. Review of major grammatical points in French.

subject: FREN
title: Intermediate Conversation and Phonetics
description: Emphasizes speaking skills, especially pronunciation. Further review of French grammar.

subject: FREN
title: Introduction to Literary Analysis in French

subject: FREN

subject: FREN

description: Study of basic French commercial terminology and institutions, in a global economic and political context.

subject: FREN
title: Topics in Modern French and Francophone Literature
description: Close reading and analysis of modern and contemporary literary texts in French.

subject: FREN

Comment(s): Open to non-majors. Credit toward a major or minor in French available with additional reading and writing in French to students who have completed FREN 353* or the equivalent.

subject: FREN
title: Phonetics
description: Foundation in the science of phonetics. Practical exercises and individual performance. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FREN 333*

subject: FREN
title: Advanced Grammar
description: Improving one’s written French by studying basic and more refined structures of the French language. Writing creative free-style compositions. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FREN 334* and FREN 353*

subject: FREN
title: French and Francophone Women Writers
description: Works by women writing in French from the Middle Ages to the present, considered in the context of French and Anglophone gender theory.

subject: FREN
title: Capstone Experience in French
description: Synthesizing senior colloquium and tutorial in which students reflect on the raison d’être of the discipline from a multidimensional point of view. (RE) Prerequisite(s): 3 hours of course work in French at the 400 level or permission of department. Registration Restriction(s): Minimum student level – junior.

subject: FREN
title: Special Topics in French and Francophone Literature
description: Selected topics in French studies. Repeatability: May be repeated if topic differs. Maximum 9 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FREN 353*

subject: FREN
title: Special Topics in French and Francophone History and Culture
description: Selected topics in French studies. Repeatability: May be repeated if topic differs. Maximum 9 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FREN 353*

subject: FREN

title: Internship
description: Career-related experiences in the United States or abroad. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 15 hours. Registration Restriction(s): French major/language and world business concentration.

description: In these seminars, students will engage in active and experiential learning with UT faculty. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 2 hours.

subject: FYS
title: Peer Mentor Techniques
description: Training of upper-class students as mentors and advisors for freshmen. Includes cognitive and developmental theories of the college-age student, teaching and learning styles, group communication and listening techniques, and mentoring and advising skills. Registration Permission: Consent of department.

subject: FYS
title: Peer Mentor Practicum
description: Peer mentoring of first year studies students. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): FYS 401 . Registration Permission: Consent of department.

subject: GAME

description: Introduction to Game Craft is an immersive and hands-on course designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of game design, development, and interactive storytelling. subject: GAME

description: Interactive and Immersive Game Experience Design is an advanced course that explores the principles and techniques of creating compelling, interactive, and immersive gaming experiences. This course goes beyond basic game design concepts, focusing on the integration of emerging technologies, storytelling, and user engagement. subject: GAME

description: Collaborative Game Design is an intermediate-level course that focuses on the collaborative and interdisciplinary aspects of designing digital games. subject: GEOG
title: World Geography
description: Survey of world regions and regional issues. Illustrates geographical points of view, concepts, and techniques.

subject: GEOG
title: Digital Earth: Maps, Society, and Environment
description: Introduces students to the foundations of spatial data, cartography, and geographic analysis. The course combines quantitative approaches to mapping with critical perspectives on how geographic information shapes our understanding of society and the environment. Students will explore a variety of geographic methods through hands-on work with geospatial datasets and accessible tools. Topics include

subject: GEOG
title: Sustainable Human Geographies
description: Introduction to key topics and core concepts in human geography. Human activities, their organization, and their impacts on the landscape.

subject: GEOG
title: Weather, Climate, and Climate Change
description: Characteristics and processes of the earth’s surface and lower atmosphere; their interaction to produce a world pattern of distinctive environments significant to humanity. Covers elements and controls of climate, atmospheric circulation, precipitation and storms, the hydrological cycle, world climate and vegetation patterns, and climate change.

subject: GEOG
title: Landscapes and Environmental Change
description: Characteristics and processes of the earth’s surface and lower atmosphere; their interaction to produce a world pattern of distinctive environments significant to humanity. Covers earth materials, tectonic activity, geomorphic processes and landforms, soils, and human impacts on the landscape.

subject: GEOG
title: Honors: Weather, Climate, and Climate Change
description: Honors-level introduction to physical geography, emphasizing characteristics and processes of the earth’s surface and lower atmosphere and their interaction to produce a world pattern of distinctive environments significant to humanity. Covers elements and controls of climate, atmospheric circulation, precipitation and storms, the hydrological cycle, world climate and vegetation patterns, and clim

subject: GEOG
title: Honors: Landscapes and Environmental Change
description: Honors-level introduction to physical geography, emphasizing characteristics and processes of the earth’s surface and lower atmosphere and their interaction to produce a world pattern of distinctive environments significant to humanity. Covers earth materials, tectonic activity, geomorphic processes and landforms, soils, and human impacts on the landscape.

subject: GEOG
title: Environmental Issues in National Parks
description: Major environmental issues faced by national parks and other protected areas in the U.S. and abroad, including invasive species, changes in fire regimes, water and air pollution, visitor impacts, and climate change. Focus on interactions between physical and biological processes and human activities.

subject: GEOG
title: Effective Science Communication for Geography and Sustainability Professionals
description: This course is focused on techniques for effective public scholarship to diverse audiences. Students will learn a variety of written and oral communication forms through individual and group assignments on communicating technical science, managing public messaging, and responding to topical themes that Geography and Sustainability professionals will encounter.

subject: GEOG
title: Understanding Climate Change
description: Overview of natural and human-caused mechanisms that have contributed to changes in Earth’s climate, with an emphasis on climate change in the 20th and 21st centuries. Discussions focus on causes, mitigation, public attitudes, and government policy.

subject: GEOG
title: Tennessee Tornadoes
description: Study of tornadoes in Tennessee, emphasizing climatological and meteorological processes and patterns. Recent events serve as case studies to analyze atmospheric conditions, forecast accuracy, early warning systems, and community vulnerability.

subject: GEOG
title: Sustainability Principles and Practices
description: This course is an introduction to theories and practices in sustainability. The course explores the connections between environmental, social, and economic systems at local, regional, and global scales. This course provides a foundational discussion into various systems including water, energy, waste, food and agriculture, pollution and production, and the built environment. (Same as EEPS 206* )

subject: GEOG
title: Sustainability Service-Learning
description: This course is an introduction to theories and practices in sustainability. The course explores the connections between environmental, social, and economic systems at local, regional, and global scales. This course is designated as a Service-Learning course and provides experiential learning opportunities for students through service projects with community partners.

subject: GEOG
title: Geography of Country Music
description: This course offers an analysis of the cultural geography and political economy of country music, with a special emphasis on the themes of urbanization, deindustrialization, and agrarian change. The course explores how country music, and economies of cultural production more generally, intersect with issues of cultural identity, industrial change, and urban-rural relations in the United States and

subject: GEOG
title: Special Topics
description: Instructor-initiated course on selected research-related topics. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: GEOG
title: Geovisualization and Geographic Information Science
description: Basic concepts and methods of geovisualization and geographic information science, including properties, sources, uses, design, and production of maps and basic spatial analysis functions.

subject: GEOG
title: First Steps in GIS Programming
description: For first-time GIS programmers. Design and implement simple to complex sequences of calculations on geospatial information. Use Python scripts to automate GIS data preparation, analysis, and mapping. Contact Hour Distribution: 2 hours lecture, 2 hours lab. Grading Restriction: Letter grade only. Recommended Background: Prior or concurrent course in geographic information systems (GIS).

subject: GEOG
title: Geospatial Field Methods of UAVs, LiDAR, and GPS
description: This course is a field and laboratory-based course to teach students how to use UAVs, LiDAR, and GPS to obtain, process, and analyze geospatial data. It will include local partners to work on a project during the semester. (DE) Prerequisite(s): GEOG 311* or consent of instructor.

subject: GEOG
title: Introduction to Uncrewed Aerial Systems
description: Provides knowledge about the regulations and procedures governing the legal operation of Small Uncrewed Aerial Systems (sUAS) in the United States of America. Introduces the fundamentals of flying drones (or sUAS) with a focus on flight proficiency skills, safety procedures, mission planning best practices, and image acquisition procedures. Recommended Background: Prior course experience in GIS

subject: GEOG
title: Special Topics in GIST
description: Detailed study of a specialized area of Geographic Information Science and Technology (GIST). Topics vary by semester. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 9 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor

subject: GEOG
title: Cultural Geography: Core Concepts
description: Background and method of cultural geography. Basic concepts and theories focusing on cultural landscape, culture regions, cultural ecology, innovation and diffusion, cultural integration, and world patterns of cultural phenomena.

subject: GEOG
title: Natural Hazards
description: Overview of earth’s natural hazards. Topics include hurricanes, earthquakes, tornadoes, severe weather, mass movements, volcanoes, tsunami, and wildfires. Hazard awareness is emphasized by highlighting case studies and important past events.

subject: GEOG
title: Climate Change and Human Response
description: Controversies and uncertainties about present-day climate change, future climate scenarios and mitigation strategies, and individual and policy responses to climate predictions. (DE) Prerequisite(s): GEOG 131*

subject: GEOG
title: Meteorology
description: Dynamic atmosphere and resulting weather events. Labs focus on the analysis of weather patterns using meteorological tools to develop and communicate a forecast.

subject: GEOG
title: Economic Geography in the Modern World
description: Concepts, theories, and changing practices and processes of economic activities in a globally interconnected and modernizing world.

subject: GEOG
title: Introduction to Urban Studies: Social and Spatial Origins of Contemporary Cities
description: Geographical and theoretical examination of models and concepts for socio-cultural changes occurring over time in contemporary urban spaces due to industrialization, globalization, and changing economic landscapes at various scales.

subject: GEOG
title: Population Geography
description: Overview of population issues around the world. Regional fertility and mortality, disease, international migration, refugees and internal displacement.

subject: GEOG
title: People and Environment
description: Spatial and temporal patterns in human use and alteration of the environment. Geographical variations in human-environment interactions, management, resource use, and stewardship. In-depth study of how humans shape Earth’s environments and are shaped by them.

subject: GEOG
title: Energy, Governance, and Sustainability
description: Comprehensive survey course to understand the role of energy resources in shaping social, political, and economic change. This course focuses specific attention on the changing geographies and governance of energy in response to climate change and addresses relatedquestions of environmental and energy justice.

subject: GEOG

subject: GEOG

subject: GEOG
title: Regional Dynamics of the United States and Canada
description: Regional explorations of changes in the cultural, economic, social, and physical landscapes of Canada and the United States, and their impacts.

subject: GEOG
title: Sustainable Development in Appalachia
description: Political economy and sustainable development issues in Appalachia with special emphasis on economic transition and current community work.

subject: GEOG
title: Southern Spaces and Places
description: Geographical appraisal of the southeastern United States, including physical environment and human resources. Origin and development of contemporary economic and cultural traits of the area.

subject: GEOG

subject: MUCO

subject: MUCO

description: An introduction to music within expressive culture and as a part of peoples’ daily lives around the world. Focuses on music as sound, its role in conceptions of identity, migration and global social processes, personal and community memory, and politics and power.

description: Keyboard skills in reading hymn texture, improvisation, harmonizing with secondary dominants, transposition, and accompaniments for major instrument. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUKB 120 .

subject: MUKB
title: Class Piano IV
description: Completes the piano competency requirement. Open score reading, 203 accompaniments for the major instrument. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUKB 210 .

subject: MUKB
title: Keyboard Skills
description: Harmonization, sight-reading, transposition, technical work, figured bass realization, and improvisation at the piano. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 120 .

subject: MUKB
title: Organ Practicum
description: Improvisation, hymn playing, and accompanying on the organ. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 hours. Recommended Background: Organ proficiency at the 200 level.

subject: MUKB
title: Introduction to Piano Technology
description: A practical study and hands on instruction in the practice of tuning, preparation, repair and maintenance of pianos. (DE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 100* and MUKB 100 , or equivalent knowledge verified by instructor screening interview. Registration Permission: Instructor permission required

subject: MUKB
title: Piano Literature I
description: From 1750 to the middle 19th century.

subject: MUKB
title: Piano Literature II
description: Middle 19th century to the present.

subject: MUKB
title: Piano Pedagogy
description: Course description: A study of piano teaching materials, pedagogical composers, methods of teaching music reading, rhythm, technique, and business practices in piano teaching.

subject: MUKB
title: The Organ and Its Literature
description: A survey course of the development of the organ and organ literature from the Middle Ages to the current day. Problems of style and interpretation.

subject: MUKB
title: Teaching Class Piano
description: Historical survey and evaluation of teaching materials and methodology for college and/or adult beginning piano classes with collateral teaching experience.

subject: MUKB
title: Internship

subject: MUPR
title: Foundations of Drumset I
description: Introductory online drumset study with emphasis on coordination, basic grooves, and timekeeping. Students learn foundational beats in contemporary popular styles while developing proper setup, posture, and practice habits. No prior drumming experience required. Contact Hour Distribution: 1/2 hour lab; 1/2 hour lecture Grading Restriction: ABC/No Credit Comment(s): Students will need to supply thei

subject: MUPR
title: Foundations of Drumset II
description: Beginner-to-intermediate drumset study designed to broaden skills and explore a wider range of styles. Students expand their groove vocabulary, develop coordination and dynamic control, and learn approaches to linear patterns, fills, and creative variations. Improvisation is introduced through short exercises that encourage personal expression. This course is a continuation of Drumset I but also p

subject: MUPR
title: Foundations of Drumset III
description: Beginner-to-intermediate drumset study emphasizing stylistic influence, transcription, and creative application. Students explore grooves and performance approaches from a variety of genres and apply them through short solo studies and creative exercises. Improvisation is introduced in guided steps, encouraging students to begin shaping their own musical voice. This course serves as both a continu

subject: MUPR
title: Pop Drumming: Modern Trends & Influences
description: Survey of drumming and percussion in popular music, focusing on how groove and rhythm shape sound, style, and trends across genres and eras. Through guided listening, students explore the role of drummers in shaping modern music. No prerequisites; open to all students.

subject: MUPR
title: Percussion History and Literature I
description: Topics pertaining to drums and percussion repertoire, instruments, industry, and techniques within historical and cultural contexts, from the early through mid-twentieth century.

subject: MUPR
title: Percussion History and Literature II
description: Topics pertaining to drums and percussion repertoire, instruments, industry, and techniques within historical and cultural contexts, from the mid-twentieth through the early twenty-first century.

subject: MUPR
title: Percussion Pedagogy I
description: Survey of resources related to teaching percussion across demographics.

subject: MUPR
title: Percussion Pedagogy II
description: Survey and application of curricula and concepts, related to teaching percussion across demographics.

subject: MUSC
title: The College of Music Experience
description: Introduction to the College of Music and UT, including resources provided and opportunities available to music students. Intended for freshmen students. Grading Restriction: ABC/N grading only. Credit Restriction: Students may not receive credit for both MUSC 100 and FYS 101 or BUAD 100 . Registration Restriction(s): Majors or minors in the College of Music.

subject: MUSC
title: Fundamentals of Performance
description: Private instrumental or vocal study, one or two half lessons per week. This course is designed to prepare students for enrollment in Music Performance 103-195. Requires payment of applied music fees. Grading Restriction: Letter grade only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 12 hours. Credit Restriction: Cannot be used to satisfy applied music requirements at the principal level for the music

subject: MUSC
title: Practice Technique
description: Scientific approach to practice strategies through the guidance of a professional practice coach. Involves a weekly lecture and practical application lab. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 2 times. (RE) Corequisite(s): Any MUPF course

subject: MUSC
title: Foundations of Guitar I - Basic Skills
description: An introduction to playing the guitar including navigating the fretboard, hand techniques, sheet music reading, and rhythmic/strumming patterns.

subject: MUSC
title: Foundations of Guitar II - Intermediate Skills
description: A continuation to the learning of guitar techniques including chords, scales, arpeggios, picking techniques, right hand techniques.

subject: MUSC
title: Foundations of Guitar III - Styles
description: Introduction to characteristic styles of guitar greats such as Jimi Hendrix, Wes Montgomery, Buddy Guy, Stevie Ray Vaughn, Eddie Van Halen, Pat Metheny. Includes the composition and recording of a riff and/or solo that incorporates the style of a selected guitarist.

subject: MUSC
title: Analysis and Public Discourse of Taylor Swift’s Music
description: Album-by-album analysis of Taylor Swift’s music covering musical, social, and media elements. Creation of a final product based on that analysis for relevant online platforms, such as a podcast or YouTube video. Students will asynchronously participate in collegial discourse as they create both group projects and the larger social discourse final project.

subject: MUSC
title: Studio Class
description: A multi-topic course focused on all aspects of performance and pedagogy. Course topics may include performances, masterclasses, guest artists, topical discussions, presentations, performance techniques, and other topics at the professor’s discretion. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No credit Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 14 times.

subject: MUSC
title: Performance Technique
description: Scientific approach to performance strategies through the guidance of a professional practice coach. Involves a weekly lecture and practical application lab. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 2 times. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUSC 102 (RE) Corequisite(s): Any MUPF course

subject: MUSC
title: Junior Recital
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 times. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 120 and MUCO 110* (RE) Corequisite(s): MUTH 140 and any 300-level or above music performance course.

subject: MUSC
title: The Evolution of Gospel Music
description: Traces the roots of Gospel music from 18th century English hymnody up through the blues to contemporary popular music. (Same as REST 314 and AFST 314 )

subject: MUSC
title: A Musician’s Life I
description: Topics and projects for today’s professional musician. Topics may include personal finance, stress management, wellness, nutrition, building websites, basic recording skills, branding and social media presence, etc. (RE) Corequisite(s): Any 300-level or above music performance course.

subject: MUSC
title: A Musician’s Life II
description: Topics and projects for today’s professional musician. Topics may include contracts; forming corporations and nonprofits; grant writing; fundraising; commissions; and performance, recording, and publishing legal matters. (RE) Corequisite(s): Any 300-level or above music performance course.

subject: MUSC
title: Senior Recital
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 times. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 220* and MUCO 210* and MUCO 220* (RE) Corequisite(s): MUTH 240 and any 400-level or above music performance course.

subject: MUSC
title: Study Abroad Experience in Music
description: Capstone project for students who have studied music abroad during their program at UTK. Students will present a summary of solutions to contemporary issues they encountered during their study abroad experience and communicate them to an audience. Registration Permission: Departmental permission required.

subject: MUSC
title: Lecture Recital
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 3 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 120 and MUCO 110* (RE) Corequisite(s): Any 200-level or above music performance course.

subject: MUSC
title: Special Topics in Performance
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 12 hours.

subject: MUSC
title: Special Topics in Pedagogy
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 4 hours.

subject: MUSC
title: Independent Study
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 30 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: MUSC
title: Sacred Music Internship
description: Observation, participation, and supervised leadership experience in the music program of an approved local church. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Registration Restriction(s): Bachelor of Music – music major – scared music concentration; minimum student level – senior.

subject: MUSC
title: Honors Senior Project
description: Completion of a project for the honors program. Projects may take the form of an additional recital, a recital paper, a curriculum proposal, or a research paper suitable for publication or presentation at a conference. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. Registration Restriction(s): Admission to music honors program.

subject: MUTC
title: Sound Recording Techniques
description: Theory and applications of tape recording’s sound reproduction and reinforcement systems. Topics include room acoustics, audio measurements, microphones, studio and real-time processing, noise reduction, mixing, editing, monitors, system wiring, and maintenance.

subject: MUTC
title: The Art of Sound Design
description: Introduction to the world of sound design including the development of the ability to critically analyze and create cohesive soundscapes that align with visual narratives.

subject: MUTC
title: Data Driven Soundscapes
description: Variable topics in music generation, using Supercollider. Includes the generation of music informed by data, the exploration of the potential of using algorithms to generate sound, the basics of Supercollider, and the incorporation of data into the music generation process.

subject: MUTC
title: Film Scoring
description: Development of basic musical and technological skills required to compose music for use with visual media. Projects may include a theme for a television program, an introductory theme for a film, music for a pre-existing action scene, music for a pre-existing commercial, and music for a short film or animation. Also includes an overview of masterpieces of media scoring. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTC

subject: MUTC
title: Commercial Scoring for Media
description: Project-based course providing enhanced understanding of modern music technology and production. Provides real-world experience in applying these principles to scoring and editing licensed music to short form media. (RE) Corequisite(s): MUTH 100* or MUTH 115* Comment(s): Consent of Instructor required. Experience with digital audio workstations suggested but not required.

subject: MUTC
title: Virtual Audio Modeling
description: Development of the basic musical and technological skills required to create models or “mock-ups” of concert music scores via DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) and sample library technology. Projects will include models of students’ own works as well as those of chamber and large form masterworks from the canon. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTC 340 , and MUPF 295 , and MUTH 120 and MUTH 140 .

subject: MUTC
title: Interactive Game Audio
description: Project-based course in building audio files and music for gaming with a focus on varying technologies and practices. Real-world experience in working with digital audio workstations, sound editing software, and authoring software that centralize all aspects of audio creation for interactive game music. Experience with digital audio workstations suggested. Repeatability: May be repeated once (RE)

subject: MUTC
title: Introduction to Computer Music Transcription
description: Exercise in notation, playback, and publishing incorporating elements of word processing, graphic design, sequencing, and page layout. Study of Music Instrument Digital Interface protocol as it applies to computer music work station design. Recommended Background: MUTH 100* or equivalent.

subject: MUTC
title: Sound Synthesis Techniques
description: Studio and real-time applications of synthesizers. Historical background, theoretical concepts, equipment interface and usage, analysis of sounds and compositions.

subject: MUTC
title: Computer Projects
description: Variable topics. Topics may include high-level programming of computer-managed instructional materials; development of Internet resources including web pages; use of recording and mixing software. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: MUTC
title: Special Topics in Music Technology
description: Intensive study in a particular area of music technology. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 9 hours.

subject: MUTC
title: Independent Study
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 30 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: MUTH
title: Fundamentals of Music
description: Theory and practice of basic elements of music.

subject: MUTH
title: Theory Workshop
description: Tutoring for students needing additional help in theory classes. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 10 times.

subject: MUTH
title: Theory I
description: Materials of music, including basic elements through non-chord tones and 6/4 chords. Exercises in analysis, composition, and improvisation of music with emphasis on common practice. Recommended Background: Successful completion of music theory placement test.

subject: MUTH
title: Harmony and Analysis through Popular Music
description: Materials of popular and commercial music including melody, harmony, rhythm, and form. Exercises in song construction, analysis, and writing about music with an emphasis on popular music of a wide variety of styles.

subject: MUTH
title: Theory II
description: Materials of music through secondary dominants and modulation. Exercises in analysis, composition, and improvisation of music with emphasis on common practice. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 110 . Comment(s): Grade of C or better in MUTH 110 is required.

subject: MUTH
title: Ear Training I
description: Development of proficiency in sight singing short melodies and identifying melodic intervals, scales, triads, and the dictation of short diatonic melodic models. Contact Hour Distribution: Includes lab hours. Grading Restriction: ABC/NC grading only. (RE) Corequisite(s): MUKB 110 . Comment(s): Grade of C or better in MUTH 100* is required.

subject: MUTH
title: Ear Training II
description: Development of proficiency in sight singing longer melodies and identifying harmonic intervals, triads, cadence types, and the dictation of longer diatonic melodic models. Contact Hour Distribution: Includes lab hours. Grading Restriction: ABC/NC grading only. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 130 . Comment(s): Grade of C or better in MUTH 130 is required.

subject: MUTH
title: Theory III
description: Materials of music through chromatic harmony and modulation. Exercises in analysis, composition, and improvisation of music with emphasis on common practice.

subject: MUTH
title: Theory IV
description: Materials of music from the dissolution of functional harmony to contemporary compositional techniques. Exercises in analysis, composition, and improvisation of music.

subject: MUTH
title: Advanced Ear Training III
description: Development of proficiency in sight singing melodies, and identifying seventh chords. Dictation of diatonic harmonic progressions and diatonic melodic models. Contact Hour Distribution: Includes lab hours. Grading Restriction: ABC/NC grading only. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 140 . Comment(s): Grade of C or better in MUTH 140 is required.

subject: MUTH
title: Advanced Ear Training IV
description: Development of proficiency in sight singing melodies. Dictation of diatonic harmonic progressions and melodic models. Contact Hour Distribution: Includes lab hours. Grading Restriction: ABC/NC grading only. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 230 . Comment(s): Grade of C or better in MUTH 230 is required.

subject: MUTH
title: Composition Class
description: An introduction to compositional techniques. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 4 hours. Comment(s): Requires interview with theory/composition faculty. Registration Restriction(s): Bachelor of Music or Bachelor of Arts – Music Major or Music Minor.

subject: MUTH
title: Composition Seminar
description: Students will build on compositional techniques and strategies learned in MUTH 250 in a masterclass setting combining individual instruction with lateral learning/input. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 250 taken twice.

subject: MUTH
title: Italian Musical Styles
description: Fundamental style and analysis of Italian music of the common practice period through today. Important stylistic and compositional trends in Italian music that lead to significant Western cultural impacts in music, such as the polyphony of the Italian Renaissance, ornamentation and improvisation in Baroque Italy, and Italian Romantic operatic forms and styles. Discussion of 20th century styles inc

subject: MUTH
title: Popular Music Style and Analysis
description: Study of the musical features of popular music across a broad spectrum of styles including country, rock, hip-hop, punk, progressive rock, metal, grunge, rap, pop, and more using a variety of analytical methods synthesized to understand meaning, style, and interpretation.

subject: MUTH
title: Form and Analysis
description: Study and practice in analysis of forms of music from smallest structural units to large compound forms. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210* and MUTH 230

subject: MUTH
title: Film Score Analysis
description: Explores the reciprocal relationship between music and film in Hollywood cinema from the past 100 years. Includes theoretical readings, practical analyses, score study, and assigned viewings of clips and complete movies. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210*

subject: MUTH
title: Instrumentation
description: Basic techniques in scoring for voice, brass, woodwind and string choirs, and percussion. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210* and MUTH 230

subject: MUTH
title: Songwriting
description: Introduction to the basics of songwriting.

subject: MUTH
title: Survey of Music Theory
description: Emphasis on harmonic practice of Baroque, Classic, and Romantic periods. Exercises in writing and analysis. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No credit only Credit Restriction: Does not count toward graduate credit. Comment(s): Recommended as a review course for graduate students.

subject: MUTH
title: Ear Training Review
description: Review and application of harmonic and melodic dictation skills. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No Credit grading only. Credit Restriction: Does not count toward graduate credit. Recommended Background: MUTH 240 . Comment(s): Recommended as a review course for graduate students.

subject: MUTH
title: How to Learn Jazz in 10 Days
description: Introduction to jazz theory and styles with application to performance and analysis. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210*

subject: MUTH
title: Orchestration
description: Advanced techniques in instrumental writing with emphasis on scoring for the concert orchestra. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210* * and MUTH 230 .

subject: MUTH
title: Counterpoint I
description: Study of species counterpoint in modal and tonal styles with emphasis on works of Palestrina and J.S. Bach. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210* and MUTH 230

subject: MUTH
title: Choral Arranging
description: Analysis of scores and writing of arrangements for choruses. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210* and MUTH 240

subject: MUTH
title: Special Topics in Music Theory
description: Intensive study in a particular area of music theory, analysis, or pedagogy. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 9 hours. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210*

subject: MUTH
title: Music and Mental Health
description: This course focuses on the analysis of musical portrayals of mental health, trauma, and the therapeutic process. Mental health topics and its musical portrayals come with a variety of trigger warnings including depression and suicide. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 210*

subject: MUTH
title: Music Theory Practicum
description: Experience in teaching through peer teaching and observation/critiques of teaching. Also includes theatrical improvisation exercises.

subject: MUTH
title: Independent Study in Music Theory
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 15 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of department head.

subject: MUTH
title: Senior Thesis
description: Capstone project in the Music Theory/Composition-Theory track. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUTH 220*

subject: MUVC
title: Class Voice I
description: Development of basic vocal skills. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 2 hours.

subject: MUVC
title: Vocal Coaching
description: Repeatability: May be repeated; maximum 8 times.

subject: MUVC
title: Acting for Singers
description: Rudiments of acting applied to a wide variety of styles from solo and ensemble literature for the lyric theater. Topics include physical awareness, improvisation, focus, gesture, dramatic and musical analysis, and styles of presentation (auditions and concerts). Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 4 times. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: MUVC
title: Performance Workshop
description: Repeatability: May be repeated up to 4 times.

subject: MUVC
title: Diction I
description: Sounds by phonetic symbols. Opera and art songs used for examples. Emphasis placed on Italian, English, and Spanish diction. Performance practice.

subject: MUVC
title: Diction II
description: Sounds by phonetic symbols. Opera and art songs used for examples. Emphasis placed on German, French, and Latin diction. Performance practice.

subject: MUVC
title: Opera Production
description: Supervised work on opera productions. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 12 hours. Comment(s): Requires audition.

subject: MUVC
title: Song Literature I
description: German songs.

subject: MUVC
title: Song Literature II
description: French, Italian, Russian, Scandinavian, Czechoslovakian, British, and American art songs.

subject: MUVC
title: Pedagogy I
description: Concepts and approaches to teaching singing, past and present, for all ages of voices. Registration Restriction(s): Bachelor of Music ― vocal performance, music education-vocal/vocal, and music education-vocal/keyboard concentrations only.

subject: MUVC
title: Pedagogy II
description: Vocal teaching materials. Includes collateral teaching experiences. (RE) Prerequisite(s): MUVC 450 .

subject: MUVC
title: Independent Study
description: Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 30 hours. Registration Permission: Consent of instructor.

subject: NAIS
title: Internship
description: This course provides course credit for internship work with community partners connected to Native American and Indigenous Studies. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No credit Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. Registration Permission: With NAIS Chair permission.

subject: NAIS
title: Independent Study
description: Student- or instructor-initiated independent study. Grading Restriction: Letter grade only Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours. Registration Permission: With Instructor and NAIS Chair permission.

subject: NE
title: Survey of Nuclear and Radiological Engineering
description: A survey of the breadth of opportunities in nuclear and radiological science and technology. Students will be introduced to career opportunities and areas of research that support the nuclear field. Grading Restriction: Satisfactory/No credit Registration Restriction(s): Engineering major only.

subject: NE
title: Introduction to Nuclear and Radiological Engineering
description: Introduction to topics and issues in nuclear engineering, with scientific and technical topics interspersed with discussions about policy, lifelong learning and professional responsibility/ethics. This course combines traditional lectures and class dialogue. Students will learn the fundamentals of radiation, nuclear chemistry, and physics that are needed to understand concepts of nuclear reactions

subject: NE
title: Fundamentals of Nuclear Chemistry
description: An introduction to the fundamentals of nuclear chemistry and its modern applications, particularly in nuclear medicine. This course provides a strong foundation for students pursuing studies in nuclear chemistry, radiochemistry, and related fields. By the end of the course, students will acquire the essential knowledge needed to understand and apply nuclear/radio chemistry in practical settings. T

subject: NE
title: Introduction to Radiological Engineering
description: Radiation quantities, limits and risk assessment, external and internal dosimetry, biological effects of radiation, radiation detection, radiation interactions and decay, applications. (DE) Prerequisite(s): NE 200 .

subject: NE
title: Mathematics and Computational Methods in Nuclear Engineering

(RE) Prerequisite(s): PSYC 335 . Registration Permission: Permission of instructor.

subject: PSYC

subject: PSYC

subject: PSYC

subject: PSYC
title: Theories of Counseling Psychology

subject: PSYC
title: Psychology of Gender

subject: PSYC

subject: PSYC

subject: PSYC

subject: PUBH
title: Introduction to Public Health
description: Explores foundational public health concepts, systems, and contemporary challenges, with attention to tools and strategies for improving population health. Emphasizes locating, evaluating, and communicating public health information—including the ethical use of generative AI tools—to support evidence-based practice and health promotion.

subject: PUBH
title: Introductory Epidemiology
description: Examines how epidemiologists monitor disease, investigate outbreaks, and use data to inform health promotion and policy. Topics include measures of morbidity and mortality, study designs, surveillance, and applications across infectious, chronic, social, environmental, and occupational health. subject: PUBH
title: Health of Adolescents
description: Examines risk and protective factors that shape adolescent health, including developmental, social, and environmental influences. Emphasis is placed on applying developmentally appropriate evidence-based strategies to promote healthy development and address adolescent health challenges.

subject: PUBH
title: Theory-driven Health Assessment and Planning
description: Addresses the concepts and procedures of health assessment and intervention, interpretation of assessment, processes of planning, program implementation, and program and process evaluation while utilizing foundational theories, models, and frameworks relevant to Public Health.

subject: PUBH
title: Public Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Management
description: Dynamics of emergency preparedness and response management. Emphasizes the role of public health professionals with a practical, public health focused approach.

subject: PUBH
title: Introduction to Research Methods in Public Health
description: Introduces qualitative and quantitative research methods used in public health. Topics include ethics, study design, sampling, data collection, and analysis. Students learn to evaluate existing research, design surveys, collect and interpret data, and apply findings to program evaluation, policy, and future studies.

subject: PUBH
title: Data Management in Public Health
description: Introduces essential data management skills for public health practice and research. Students learn to organize, clean, analyze, and visualize data using tools such as Microsoft Excel. Emphasis is placed on data management planning, ethical considerations, teamwork, and communicating findings to different audiences. (RE) Prerequisite(s): PUBH 201*

subject: PUBH
title: Public Health Aspects of Aging
description: Explores biological, psychological, social, and environmental factors that influence aging and the health of older adults. Topics include chronic disease, mental health, caregiving, policy, and age-friendly communities. Students analyze systems and community approaches that support healthy aging and address challenges across different contexts.

subject: PUBH
title: Death and Dying
description: The course is designed to analyze the relationship between death and health, with an emphasis on the biological, psychological, bioethical, and legal aspects of death in contemporary society. subject: PUBH

description: This course is designed to prepare students for successful experiential learning in public health settings, including internships, practicums, and other field-based experiences. Emphasis is placed on understanding healthcare system models, the influence of social and political context, and lessons that can inform efforts to improve population health outcomes.

subject: PUBH

description: Examines how international organizations, governments, NGOs, and public–private partnerships shape global health policy and interventions. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking and applying evidence to address environmental health challenges in different contexts.

subject: PUBH
title: Suicide and Suicide Prevention Across the Lifespan
description: This course examines factors that make suicide a serious public health problem across the lifespan with an emphasis on surveillance, assessment, prevention, intervention, and postvention.

subject: PUBH

subject: PYED

subject: PYED

subject: REED

subject: REST

subject: REST

description: Religions of indigenous peoples in selected contexts and the relationship of religion and culture cross-culturally. (Same as ANTH 302 .)

subject: REST
title: Sociology of Religion
description: The sociology of religion is a distinctive approach that investigates the intersection of religions and religious organizations to history, culture, and society. In this course we review the methods, theories, and substantive findings of classical and contemporary sociologists who study religion and the social order. (Same as SOCI 303* )

subject: REST
title: Topics in Religious Studies
description: Selected figures, themes, movements, and problems in Religious Studies. Variable content. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: REST

subject: REST

subject: REST
title: Religion and the Workplace
description: Within the framework of the academic study of religion, students will engage legal and organizational issues with religion in the workplace, focusing on understanding the complex dynamics that characterize workplace interactions.

Explores how religious worlds influence gameworlds and how gameworlds can inform themes germane to the study of religion. Thematic examination of topics can include: heroes, magic, powerful agents, sacred space, and world building.

subject: REST

subject: REST

description: Examines gender and sexuality in the histories, canonical texts, popular literature and film, and practices of the religions and cultures of Asia. (Same as WGS 319 .)

subject: REST
title: Gender, Sexuality, and Religion
description: This course explores how gender and sexuality are constructed, expressed, and addressed in religious history, literature and the arts, and social and political movements. (Same as WGS 320* )

subject: REST

description: Influence of pre-Christian Judaism and Greco-Roman culture and philosophy on early Christianity. Variety of early Christian teachings and texts and the formation of the New Testament. Survey of the early history of Christianity up to its adoption by the emperor Constantine. (Same as HIEU 321* ; JST 321* )

subject: REST

description: Major themes, events, texts, and figures of Christianity in the Roman and Byzantine Empires (after the New Testament period). Includes the study of early Christian controversies over topics such as gender and sexuality, Christianity and politics, interpreting scripture, and defining Christian orthodoxy. (Same as HIEU 322* )

subject: REST
title: Christianity: An Introduction
description: This course addresses major historical, cultural, and literary developments in Christianity, exploring the diversity of Christian thought and practice throughout time and around the globe.

Topics will include: the life of the Prophet Muhammad, Islamic, Sufism, ritual and practice, theology, art and literature. (Same as ASST 332* .

subject: REST

description: Examines different views and representations of the body in the Islamic tradition. Subjects covered include: religious doctrine and legal views on the body, medicine and healing practices and discourses, ritual purity, gender, sex and sexuality, Islamic spirituality, literature and the arts. (Same as MEST 335* )

subject: REST
title: Islam in the Modern World
description: This course will examine major themes and trends in Islamic thought and practice from the colonial era to the present. (Same as ASST 339* .)

subject: REST
title: Religion and Spirituality in American Literature
description: (See ENGL 341* )

subject: REST
title: Religion, Nature, and Ethics
description: An investigation of the efforts of religious communities in addressing environmental issues around the world with special emphasis on themes of environmental justice.

subject: REST
title: Religions in Appalachia
description: An examination of the history of religions in the Appalachian region with emphasis on diversity and intersections with national and global issues.

subject: REST

description: (See CLAS 345* .)

subject: REST
title: Black Power to Black Lives Matter in African American Religious Thought
description: Historical and critical examination of the formation and development of African American religious thought in conjunction with, and critical of, Black freedom movements from the Black Power Movement to the Black Lives Matter Movement.

subject: REST
title: African American Religion in the United States
description: Historical and critical examination of the formation and development of African American religious thought and institutions in America. (Same as AFST 352* )

description: Selected people, themes, movements, or problems touching on how religion in North America has been shaped by racial and ethnic diversity and conflict. Focus on African Americans and their relation to others such as Native Americans, Latino/as, and Asian Americans. Variable Content. (Same as AFST 353* .)

subject: REST

subject: REST

subject: REST

subject: REST
title: American Religious History

Special attention is also paid to the contemporary revival of NeoPagan witchcraft and other nature-oriented religious movements in contemporary American society.

subject: REST

subject: REST
title: Buddhism
description: Survey of the origins of Buddhism in India and further development of Buddhist philosophy and religion in India, China, Korea, Japan, the countries of Southeast Asia, and beyond.

subject: REST

description: An introduction to the religious traditions of China, including Confucianism, Daoism, Buddhism, and local religion, from the ancient to modern periods. Addresses themes such as politics, society, and gender.

subject: REST
title: American Buddhism
description: An overview of different forms of Buddhism in the Americas during the modern period, with attention to issues such as politics, globalization, and gender.

subject: REST

description: History, traditions, philosophy, and religion of the Jewish people grounded in the ancient period, but includes diaspora, emancipation and haskalah. (Same as JST 381* )

subject: REST

description: Traditional religious heritage and contemporary expressions of religion in Japan with attention to relationships of persons to nature, self-mastery and spontaneity, individual and community, and secular to sacred.

subject: REST

description: Renewal trends in 19th and 20th-century Judaism. (Same as JST 385 .) Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: REST

subject: RMM

Students will engage in leadership opportunities and learn how to write activity-based lesson plans and implement behavioral management strategies.

description: A critical assessment of the criminal justice apparatus and its components. Brief examination of the police, with most of the emphasis on the criminal courts and institutions and programs such as the prison, probation, and parole. Analysis of their operation and impacts.

subject: SOCI
title: Black Men in US Societies
description: (See AFST 354 .)

subject: SOCI
title: Environment and Resources
description: Relationship between scarcity of natural resources and changes in societal beliefs and social structure. Topics include social and physical limits to growth and collective action problems.

subject: SOCI
title: Environmental Justice
description: This course provides an environmental justice framework for understanding how racialized discrimination, gender, sexual orientation, income, and national origin are intrinsically connected to environmental degradation, climate change, and the failure to create a just and sustainable future for all of earth’s inhabitants.

subject: SOCI
title: Population
description: Demographic factors and social structure. Trends in fertility, mortality, population growth, migration, distribution, and composition. Population policy.

subject: SOCI
title: Food, Agriculture, and Society
description: Social and environmental dimensions of production, distribution, and consumption of food, with particular emphasis on historical and cross-national examples.

subject: SOCI
title: Gender in Society
description: Exploration of gender in society utilizing various sociological perspectives with special focus on the relationships between social structures, social roles, and gender identities. (Same as WGS 375* )

subject: SOCI
title: Political Economy of Regions and Peoples of the World
description: Examines questions of political economy in specific regions of the world. Specific topics in relation to the peoples of the region may include historical and contemporary manifestations of power, conflict, inequality, colonialism, development, postcolonialism, environmental degradation, migration, social movements, and transnationalism. (Same as GLBS 395 ) Repeatability: May be repeated (with diff

subject: SOCI
title: Special Topics
description: Variable topics. Scope of subject matter determined by students and instructor with consent of department. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: SOCI
title: Special Topics in Criminology
description: Variable topics in criminology. Scope of subject matter determined by students and instructor with consent of department. Repeatability: May be repeated. Maximum 6 hours.

subject: SOCI
title: Sociology of Culture
description: Examination of the role of culture in human social life from various theoretical perspectives. Exploration of social foundations of differentiation based on lifestyle and taste.

subject: SOCI
title: Police and Society
description: This course explores the role and function of police in society, including an emphasis on history, politics, economy, and culture. Special emphasis is placed on the relation between police power and the making of race, class, and gender dynamics and inequalities. (Same as JUST 411 )

subject: SOCI
title: Visual Criminology
description: This course explores 1) the power and spectacle of crime and punishment and how its representation shapes our popular knowledge of and policy in criminal justice; 2) the key dimensions of visual criminology, its key theories, tools, and methods; and 3) the usefulness of digital research and advocacy skills for careers in media and social justice.

subject: SOCI
title: Sociology, Science Fiction Film, and Artificial Intelligence
description: Examines how science-fiction films center on the tension between society and technology; focuses on artificial intelligence to understand the persistence of social problems and issues, via important contributions to sociology and social theory. (Same as CNST 419 ) Grading Restriction: Letter grade only

subject: SOCI
title: Applied Sociological Research
description: Survey of advanced topics in sociological research, and hands-on application of research methods. (RE) Prerequisite(s): SOCI 331* Comment(s): Encouraged for students interested in graduate school. Required for sociology honors students.

subject: SOCI
title: Participatory Action Research
description: Participatory Action Research (PAR) is a collaborative approach to research that brings together researchers and community members to identify, analyze, and act upon community challenges. In this course students will learn about the origins, processes, and epistemological underpinnings of PAR as we work with local community partners to carry out a community-based research project.

subject: SOCI
title: Comparative Poverty and Development
description: Critical examination of patterns of poverty and inequality in developing areas of the world, and review of major theories of development. (Same as AFST 442 .) Comment(s): SOCI 342 is recommended before taking SOCI 442.

subject: SOCI
title: Black Masculinities
description: (See AFST 444 .)

subject: SOCI
title: The Modern World System
description: Critical examination of the capitalist world-system as a social system, its coherence, boundaries, regions, member groups, cleavages, and patterns of conflict. Analysis of who gets what, why, and how in the global political economy.

subject: SOCI
title: Youth Justice
description: This course examines the historical and contemporary nature and social contexts of juvenile delinquency, as well as theoretical explanations of and social reactions to delinquency in American society.

subject: SOCI
title: Race, Ethnicity, Crime, and Justice
description: Examines racial/ethnic disparities in criminal offending and victimization, as well as different experiences with law enforcement, judicial, and correctional agencies. Emphasis on social justice. (Same as AFST 456 .)

subject: SOCI
title: Gender and Crime
description: Probes the gendered nature of offending, victimization, and criminal justice. Examines the different experiences of males and females, and theories that attempt to explain these differences. (Same as WGS 453* )

subject: SOCI
title: Restorative Justice
description: Explores the restorative justice perspective on crime, harm and conflict and its global practices, which recognize reparation, reconciliation, and social justice. (Same as WGS 454 )

subject: SOCI
title: Law and Society
description: How laws and legal processes are affected by social change, the social impact of legal sanctions, and relations between law and social justice. (Same as JUST 455* )

subject: SOCI
title: Punishment and Society
description: Examines theories and practices of punishment, including imprisonment, capital punishment, transnational penal trends, and social policy alternatives.

subject: SOCI
title: Honors Thesis in Sociology
description: Independent study for developing and writing the honors thesis in sociology.

subject: SOCI
title: Capitalism and Racism
description: Explores the emergence of race and racism with capitalism through an examination of capitalist geographies, institutions, racialized labor dynamics, and in resistance to various forms of domination.
